ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Installed Production Capacity of Fertilizer Plants 
* 181. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL: Will the Minister of 
CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of fertilizer/urea plants set up during the Ninth Five 
Year Plan period and those proposed to be set up during the Tenth Five 
Year Plan, State-wise and location-wise; 
(b) the installed production capacity of each of aforesaid units; and 
(c) by when, their commercial production is expected to be started? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI 
SUKHDEV SINGH DHINDSA): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
The details of major fertilizer projects in India commissioned 
during ninth plan period and under implementation at present, indicating 
their additional production capacity, location, month/year of 
commissioning etc., are given in the enclosed statement-I (See below). 
There is no decision on any fresh investment for a new unit under 
public/ co-operative sector. Se tting up of fertilizer plants in the private 
sector is not subject to any licensing requirements.

is not maintained and is also not available.

are planned well in advance. There is no length of rail length, which needs 
immediate (emergency) replacement, whic h is necessitated only in case of 
accidents or natural calamities.

THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. MURLI 
MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Trafficking of children is an offence under the Immoral Traffic 
(Prevention) Act, 1956 (ITPA), administered by the States/UTs. As per information 
readily available with us, in rescue operations in the Union Territory of Delhi 
between January 1, 2001 and 17th September, 2001, 143 girls have been rescued. 
Of these. 31 girls belonged to Andhra Pradesh; 12 each to Kamataka and Maharashtra; 
and I to Tamil Nadu. On the directions of the Delhi High Court, steps have been 
taken for their rehabilitation in consultation with respective State Governments. 
(d) The Government has taken the following steps to prevent trafficking 
of children:— 
(i) Drawn up a National Plan of Acti on (1998) and constituted a Central 
Advisory Committee to combat trafficking, rescue and rehabilitate victims of 
trafficking and commercial sexual exploitation, and activate legal and law 
enforcement systems to strengthen implementation of the ITPA. 
(ii) Set up State Advisory Committees on Trafficking for the same purpose, 
devolving authority and seeking to mobilize greater state resources in the fight 
against trafficking. 
(iii) The Department of Women & Child Development (DWCD) has issued 
guidelines to the States for effective implementation of the Plan of Action and 
regularly reviews State action. 
(iv) The DWCD is presently reviewing the existing legal framework 
including the Immoral Trafficking (Prevention) Act. 
(v) DWCD has undertaken regional efforts, in alliance with NGOs, to 
create greater awareness of the dimensions of trafficking and increase sensitivity 
to victims among Government departments, the police and judiciary, as well as 
within civil society at large.

(viii) Profiling NGOs that are engaged in tackling trafficking and helping to

(ix) The DWCD has initiated a new scheme called SWADHAR for women 
in difficult situations applicable to victims of trafficking also. The Scheme provides 
for shelter, counselling, medical assistance, vocational training to rescued victims. 
(x) DWCD has formulated a model grant-in-aid scheme for assistance to 
NGOs to combat trafficking in source areas, traditional areas and destination 
areas through prevention, rescue and rehabilitation. Emphasis is placed on 
counselling, non-formal education and vocational training. 
(xi) DWCD has notified officers of the level of Inspector and above in the 
CBI as Trafficking Police Officers for investigation of inter-state trafficking cases. 
(xii) The DWCD has proposed to the Ministry of Home Affairs to set up a 
nodal agency for combating and monitoring of trafficking. 
(xiii) The NHRC and DWCD have initiated a Survey on trafficking within 
the country. The study will also investigate the causal and behavioral aspects of 
all agents in trafficking. The DWCD has also commissioned a Survey to go into 
the magnitude of the problem, an estimate of the numbers involved and trafficking 
routes.

Fertility of Land 
†*195. SHRIMATI SAVITA S HARDA: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that fertility of land in the country is decreasing day 
by day; 
(b) if so, whether Government are considering to take any steps to control 
this trend; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI AJIT SINGH): (a) to (c) 
No, Sir. The foodgrains production in the country is steadily increasing to show 
that in general there is no decline in the soil fertility. The foodgrain production 
was 203.61 million tonnes during 1998-99, which had increased to 208.81 
million tonnes during 1999-2000. However, the decline in the foodgrain 
production during 2000-01 is attributed to drought-like situation in many 
States. The production during the current year is expected to be 210 million 
tonnes. 
There are, however, instances of declining in soil health are productivity 
due to inadequate and imbalanced use of fertilizers in certain areas of the 
country. To ensure that there is no ill- effect of any kind due to excessive and 
imbalanced use of fertilizers, the Government propagates the use of integrated 
nutrients combining chemical fertilizers, organic manures and biofertilizers on 
the basis of soil tests. 
The Government has taken following important steps to encourage the 
balanced and integrated use of plant nutrients for sustaining soil fertility:— . 
(i) The soil-testing programme is periodically strengthened to make 
the fertilizers use recommendations according to the nutrient status 
of the soils. 
(ii) Financial support is given to decontrolled phosphatic and potassic 
fertilizers so as to increase their consumption and thereby bring 
balance in NPK consumption. 
(iii) Use of integrated nutrients through chemical fertilizers including 
            micronutrients, organic sources like biofertilizers, compost/ 
vermicompost is being encouraged so as to maintain soil fertility 
and make cheaper source of plant nutrients available to the crops.

Integrating production and marketing of farm produce 
1319. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in recent report, it was stated that there was an 
urgent need to integrate production and marketing of farm produce through a 
process of reforms, to enhance price and quality competitiveness of agricultural 
products; 
43 

RAJYA SABHA [ 15 March, 2002] 
(b) whether some of the points mentioned are qualitative improvement 
by the use of better seeds and irrigation, infrastructure and prevention of wastage; 
and 
(c) if so, what are Government plans in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) An Expert Committee set up by 
the Ministry of Agriculture on Strenthening and Developing of Agricultural 
Marketing has in its report on 29th June, 2001 inter-alia recommended for 
establishment of an alternative marketing system to enhance price and quality 
competitiveness of agricultural products sold by the farmers. The forms of 
alternative marketing identified by the committee include direct marketing by 
producers, marketing through farmers interest groups, setting up of terminal 
markets by the private sector, forward markets and futures exchanges, electronic 
trading-e-commerce, setting up of mega  markets covering all marketing 
functions for domestic as well as export trade, and introduction of negotiable 
warehouse receipt system. 
(b) The Committee has recommended development of marketing 
infrastructure in the form of construction of rural roads, market yards, storage, 
rural godown, cold storages, reefer vans, value addition and processing and 
telecommunications. The Committee has also recommended creation of 
facilities for cleaning, grading, scientific packaging at the farm level to prevent 
wastage during the marketing process. 
Breeder seed production of crops is the mandate of Indian Council of 
Agricultural Research (ICAR). About 24,000 quintals of breeder seed of different 
crops in addition to that of vegetable crops, is produced every year maintaining 
the quality standards. 
(c) With a view to examine the recommendations made by the Expert 
Committee and to suggest measures to be taken for implementing them, an 
inter-Ministerial Task Force has been constituted by the Government. 
In order to stengthen the storage infrastructure in the country, a new 
Central Sector Scheme of Capital Investment Subsidy for construction/ 
renovation/expansion of Rural Godowns has been approved on 26.2.2002 to 
be implemented during 2001—03. The backended subsidy under the scheme 
is linked to institutional credit and will be available to projects financed by 
Commercial Banks, Cooperative Banks and Regional Rural Banks. The project 
for construction of rural godowns can be taken up by individual, farmers, group 
44 

[15 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
of farmers/growers, partnership/Proprietary firms, Non-Government 
Organisations, Self Help Groups, Companies, Corporations Cooperatives, 
Agricultural Produce Marketing Commi ttees. Marketing Boards and Agro 
Processing Corporations in the entire country. 
The National Horticulture Board (NHB), is implementing the scheme of 
Capital Investment Subsidy for construction/expansion/ modernisation of cold 
storage/Storages for Horticultural Produce. Under this scheme, the promoter of 
cold storage is eligible for 25% subsidy subject to a ceiling of Rs. 50 lakhs and 
subsidy @33.33% of the project cost upto a ceiling of Rs. 60 lakhs per project 
for North Eastern States. 
The Government is also providing assistance for horticulture crops to the 
farmers under the Centrally Sponsored Macro Management Scheme @50% of 
cost for small and marginal, SC & ST and Women farmers and 35% of the cost 
of other category of farmers for taking up drip irrigation.

Group on Agricultural Credit, Cooperation and Crop Insurance constituted by 
the Planning Commission have reported that the credit flow required in real 
terms to achieve the Tenth Plan growth target of 4 percent in Agriculture would 
be of the order of Rs. 736570 crores. Provision of credit to agricultural sector is

channels is expected to reach the targ eted level of Rs. 64000 crores in the

credit to farmers. These, inter-alia, include the following:—

which the Banks fix targets of agri cultural credit. As a result of 
implementation of this scheme, flow of credit to agricultural sector 
has increased from Rs. 8255 crores in 1994-95 to Rs. 24654 crores 
in 2000-01.

Banks for promoting investment in high tech areas such as 
aquaculture, floriculture, pisciculture etc., have been opened. So far 
61 such SAFBs have been opened by the Public Sector Banks.

KCCs issued upto December 31,2001 was 2.07 crores.

comprehensive risk insurance to  encourage farmers to increase 
investment in agriculture.

been set up to help the States in investing in rural infrastructure.

1351. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): Will the Minister 
of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a major port of fertilizer subsidies goes, not to

prices of Urea, and the reasons for high cost of production of Urea in India? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS AND 
FERTILIZERS (SHRI SATYA BRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) and (b) In order to 
make available fertilizer at affordable prices, the Government provides subsidy 
on urea and concession on decontrolle d phosphatic and potassic fertilizers. 
Government fixes the Maximum Retail Price (MRP) in case of urea, the only 
controlled fertilizer, and indicates MRPs in case of de-controlled P&K fertilizers. 
The MRPs of Single Super Phosphate  are indicated by respective State 
Governments. The fertilizers are sold at uniform MRP and indicative MRPs, as 
the case may be, to the farmers throughout the country, which are far less than 
the cost of production of fertilizers. The subsidy is paid to urea manufacturers 
which consequently benefits the farmers. Thus, the benefit is passed on to the 
farmers in the form of uniform and subsidized MRPs.

higher than the prevailing international rice. This is primarily on account of 
higher cost of feed stock/raw materials in India.

Fine on the Ministry of Environment and Forests 
1360. SHRI SOL1PETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Union Ministry of Environment and Forests 
has been fined twice by the Supreme Court of India recently; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, together with the reasons for imposition of 
fines by Supreme Court; and 
(c) the reasons for not taking timely and properly action by the Ministry? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): fa) to (c) In Writ Petition No. 657/1995 as per the Supreme Court's 
orders, the Ministry was required to (i) submit a report on the waste oil 
consignments seized at Jawahar Lai Nehru Port, Nhava Sheva, Mumbai, 
89 

RAJYA SABHA [ 15 March, 2002] 
(ii) conduct an inquiry regarding the disappearance of wastes from the port, 
and (iii) file an affidavit regarding action taken on the Action Plan contained in 
the report of the High Powered Committee (HPC). The Ministry has complied 
with the directions by way of filing an affidavit on 26.09.2001 based on the 
report of analysis of oil samples collected from the seized containers at Jawahar 
Lai Nehru Port, Nhava Sheva, Mumbai, carried out by the Indian Institute of 
Petroleum, Dehradun and setting up an Inquiry Committee on 31.01.2002 to 
probe into the disappearance of wastes from the ports. A detailed supplementary 
affidavit was filed on 06.12.2001 incorporating the responses of various States 
in respect of the recommendations of the HPC. Based on the above facts, an 
application has been filed in the Supreme Court Seeking condonation of the 
fine of Rs. 10000 imposed vide Supreme Court's order dated 04.02.2002. 
The Supreme Court, as per their orders dated 18.02.2002 in Interlocutory 
Application No. 566 in Writ Petition No. 202/ 95, imposed a cost of Rs. 5000 
on the Ministry for non-submission of affidavit, as directed in their orders on 
23.11.2001. The court directed this Ministry to formulate a scheme, whereby, 
whenever forest land is permitted for non-forestry use, the responsibility of 
raising compensatory afforestation should be on the user agency. The Supreme 
Court had earlier passed similar directions in Interlocutory Application No. 
574 on 08.09.2000. In compliance to the directions of 08.09.2000, this Ministry 
had submitted a detailed scheme in its affidavit of 03.01.2001 elucidating 
various options for carrying out compensatory afforestation. However, the 
attention of the Supreme Court could not be drawn to the fact that the Ministry 
has already filed the scheme, as directed by the Court in reference to Interlocutory 
Application No. 566, vide Ministry's affidavit on 03.01.2001. 
In view of the above facts, the Ministry has taken up the issue with the 
Solicitor General of India to request the Supreme Court to consider the affidavit 
already filed on 03.01.2001 and also reconsider their direction regarding cost 
imposed.

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R.

that the annual average of sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen normally 
remained well within the prescribed limit whereas the suspended particulate

No conclusive data is available to establish the co-relationship between the

(d) The steps taken by the Government to control the air pollution include 
the following:— 
(i) A comprehensive Policy for Abatement of Pollution that lays stress 
on both the control and preventive aspects of pollution has been 
formulated. 
(ii) Environmental Epidemiological Studies have been initiated in the 
different parts of the country to assess the impact of pollution on 
human health and suggest mitigative measures; 
(iii) Emission standards for on-road vehicles and mass emission 
standards for new vehicles have been notified under the Motor 
Vehicles Act, 1988 and are enforced by Transport Departments of 
the State Governments including Delhi. 
(iv) Unleaded petrol is supplied in the entire country from 1.2.2000 
and diesel with 0.25% sulphur maximum content is supplied from 
1.1.2000 in the entire country. Ultra low sulphur (0.05%) fuel (petrol 
and diesel) has also been introduced in major cities. 
(v) Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) is supplied for automobiles through 
a number of retail outlets in Delhi to cater to the CNG vehicles. 
(vi) Benzene concentration in petrol has been reduced. 
(vii) A network of 290 Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations has 
been set up throughout the country. 
(viii) Emission standards for industries have been notified under the 
Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to check pollution. 
92 

[15 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(ix) Steps have been taken to control of pollution from 17 categories of 
highly polluting industries. 
(x) Industries are also required to install necessary pollution control 
equipments before commissioning of their plants.

Pollution Control Board under the Air (Prevention and Control of 
Pollution) Act, 1981. 
Supreme Court target for cleaning Yamuna river 
1364. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BI RLA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Supreme Court had set a target for cleaning up 
of the Yamuna river; 
(b) if so, what are the details thereof; and 
(c) what progress has been made in implementation of the plan, formulated 
by Government for the purpose. 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T. R. 
BAALU:(a)Yes,Sir. 
(b) The Supreme Court in CWP No. 725/1994 vide its order dated 
11.04.2001 has directed that steps be taken so as to ensure that minimum 
desired water quality i.e. of class 'C' be obtained in River Yamuna at least by 
March 31, 2003. 
(c) The progress made in the implementation of the plan along with the 
proposed actions is as follows:— 
(i) A ugmentation of Sewage treatment capacity: The installed capacity 
of the STP has been augmented from 1290 million litre per day in 
1995 to 2190 million litre per day. It is targeted to be increased to 
2258 million litre per day by March, 2002 and further to 2326 
million litre per day by September, 2002. The sewage treatment 
capacity is proposed to be augmented to 3225 million litre per day 
by 10th Five Year Plan. These plants are to be designed to meet 
better standards i.e. Biological Oxygen Demand of 10 milligram 
per litre, suspended solids of 15 milligram per litre and coliforms 
less than 1,000 *MPN/100 millilitre. 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [ 15 March, 2002] 
(ii) Desilting and rehabilitation of Trunk Sewers: An Action Plan for 
desilting and rehabilitation of Trunk  Sewers has been prepared. 
Works are planned to be completed by September, 2003. So far, 18 
km. of sewers have been desilted/repaired. 
(iii) Laying of sewer lines in unauthorised/regularised colonies: Out of 
567 unauthorised/regularised colonies, sewer lines have been laid in 
418 colonies. Sewer lines will be laid in the remaining colonies by 
the year 2004 according to sewage generation in these colonies. 
(iv) Laying of sewer lines in Resettlement colonies: Out of 44 resettlement 
colonies, sewerage facilities have been provided in 40 colonies. 
Sewer lines in remaining colonies will be completed by 2004. 
(v) Laying of sewer lines in urban villages: Out of 135 urban villages, 
93 urban villages have been sewered so far. Sewerage facilities in 
all the remaining urban villages are to be provided by year 2004 
according to sewage generation in these colonies. 
(vi) Upgradation of existing STPs: The existing plants and plants under 
construction will be upgraded to meet more stringent standards of 
Biochemical Oxygen Demand of 10 milligram per litre, suspended 
solids of 15 milligram per litre and coliforms of less than 1000 *MPN/ 
100 millilitre. 
(vii) Replacement of undersized sewers: A scheme has been prepared to 
replace 585 km. undersized sewers by 250 mm diameter sewers by 
the year 2005 at a tota l cost of Rs. 140 crore out of which 68 km 
length has been replaced. 
(viii). Trapping of drains: An action plan has been prepared for trapping 
of storm water drains into sewerage system thus minimising the 
flow of untreated waste water into river Yamuna. 
(ix) Construction of Community Toilet Complexes: A project for Rs. 167 
crores for construction of 1146 toilet complexes and decentralised 
mini sewage treatment plants has been taken up. This will take care 
of the problems of disposal of sewage and sullage in about 1100 
Jhugie-Jhopri clusters and 46 Jhugie-Jhopri resettlement colonies. 
(x) Shifting of Jhugies from the bank of river/drains: For shifting of 
62,000 Jhugie-Jhopri from the embankment of the river/major 
drains, a proposal amounting to Rs. 600 crores has been prepared.

ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the C&AG, in its recent report, has revealed shortcomings in 
implementation of Water (Prevention & Control of Pollution) Act, 1974; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether water pollution in the country is increasing and various 
agencies have totally failed to check such trend; and 
(d) if so, the concrete steps Government propose to take to enforce the 
Act, effectively? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) The Comptroller and Auditor General's Report indicated 
gaps in implementation of programmes relating to pollution prevention, control 
and abatement of water pollution and performance of Pollution Control Boards. 
(c) and (d) The Pollution Control Boards have been able to control 
pollution through various preventive, promotional and mitigative measures. 
The initiatives taken by the Pollution Control Boards have resulted in reduction 
of pollution from different sources. The steps taken to check water pollution 
and to enforce the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 
effectively include the following:— 
(i) Technical and financial support has been provided for 
strengthening of Pollution Control Boards (PCBs) and Pollution 
Control Committees (PCCs). 
(ii) Periodic interaction meetings are held with the personnel at various 
levels of the Pollution Control Boards (PCBs) and Pollution 
Control Committees (PCCs). 
(iii)   State Governments have been advised to induct professionals in 
the Pollution Control Boards and Pollution Control Committees. 
(iv) State Governments have been advised to lift the ban on recruitment 
of scientific and technical personnel for the Pollution Control Boards. 
(v) Guidelines have been framed for streamlining the procedure for 
issuance of consent and authorization by the Pollution Control 
Boards. 
95 

RAJYA SABHA [ 15 March, 2002] 
(vi) Minimal National Standards for control of pollution from various 
sources have been laid down by the Central Pollution Control 
Board for implementation through the concerned State Pollution 
Control Boards. 
(vii) Effluent standards have been notified for 71 different categories of 
industries. 
(viii) Water quality at 507 monitoring stations carried out by State Pollution 
Control Board have been review ed and data used for executing 
programmes on abatement of pollution in rivers and lakes. 
(ix) The Ganga Action Plan and National River Conservation Plan have 
been launched on the basis of survey of water quality and river 
basin surveys conducted by CPCB and SPCBs. 
(x) For ground water protection, the Central Ground Water Authority 
has been set up. 
(xi) For coastal water, with the support of Ocean Development, a national 
programme has been taken along with concerned SPCBs. 
(xii) Central/Pollution Control Board (CPCB) directed the State Pollution 
Control Boards/Pollution control committees for identification of 
grossly polluting industries discharging their effluents directly into 
the rivers and for taking action against those which have not provided 
the requisite Effluent Treatment Plants (ETPs).

Treatment Plants (CETPs) in cluster of small-scale industries.

(c) Poaching is considered to be a major threat to many species of wild

(d) The steps taken to prevent poaching of wild animals are as follows:— 
(1) Action taken at the State level: 
(i) Legal protection has been provided to tigers and other wild animals 
against hunting and commercial exploitation under the provisions 
of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. 
(ii) State level and District level coordination committees have been set 
up in several States to prevent poaching and illegal trade in 
wildlife. 
(2) Action taken at National level 
(i) During the IXth Five Year Plan , the Government has increased the

the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to apprehend and prosecute 
wildlife offenders. Anti-poaching efforts are being coordinated with 
INTERPOL.

various Centrally Sponsored Schemes, viz. Project Tiger, Project 
Elephant, Development of National Parks and Sanctuaries and Eco-
development around Protected Areas for enhancing the capacity 
and infrastructure of the States for providing effective protection 
to wild animals. Financial assistance is, in particular, being provided

poachers and smugglers.

(vi) A Special Coordination and Enforcement Committee has been set up under 
the chairmanship of Secretary, Environment & Forests, Government of 
India, for control of poaching and illegal trade in wildlife. 
(vii) Export of wild animals and their derivatives is prohibited under EXIM 
policy. 
(viii) A National Conference of Forests and Environment Ministers of State 
Government was held on 29th and 30th January, 2001. It was resolved to 
organise existing protection staff into viable formations for effective 
control of poaching and to create enforcement infrastructure both 
within and out side protected areas. 
(ix) Ministry of Home Affairs has written to all the State Governments to lend a 
helping hand to the field formations to curb poaching and illegal trade in 
wildlife. 
(x) A meeting of Tiger Enforcement Task Force of CITES was organized during 
April, 2001 in Delhi to work out a strategy for controlling illegal trade 
in tiger parts and products. 
(3) Action taken at International level. 
(i) Government of India seeks international co-operation under the 
provisions.of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species 
of Wild Flora and Fauna (CITES) for control of illegal trade in 
wildlife items. 
(ii) To control transboundary trade a protocol has been signed with Peoples' 
Republic of China and a MoU has been signed with His Majesty's 
Government of Nepal.

Statement-I 
The Details of the Wildlife Conservation Stretegy-2002 adopted by the 
Indian Board for Wildlife 
1. Wildlife and forests shall be declared priority sector at the national level 
for which funds should be earmarked. 
2. Law enforcement agencies must ensure that those engaged in poaching, 
illicit trade in wildlife and wildlife products, destruction of their habitat, 
and such other illegal activities are given quick and deterrent 
punishment. 
3. We should fully tap the potential in wildlife tourism and at the same time 
take care that it does not have advers e impact in wildlife and protected 
areas. The revenue earned from increased tourism should be used entirely 
to augment available resources for conservation. 
4. Protecting interests of the poor and tribals living around protected areas 
should be handled with sensitivity and with maximum participation of 
the affected people. They should have access to the minor forest produce, 
in the forest outside of national parks and sanctuaries. Employment and 
means generation for these people is crucial for maintaining symbiosis 
between the forests, wildlife and the people. People should be encouraged 
to take up afforestation and conservation in new areas. 
5. While strengthening protective measures against traditional threats to 
wildlife, we should also respond to newer threats such as toxic chemicals 
and pesticides. 
 
6. There should be greater governmental as well as societal recognition and 
support for the many non-governmental organizations engaged in wildlife 
conservation. Mainstream media to better highlight their activities as 
also successes of governmental initiative that have worked. 
7. Creatively produced Television Programmes on wildlife and ecology 
are wildely appreciated by young and old as seen from the popularity of 
dedicated T.V. channels like, Discovery, National Geographic and 
Animal Planet. It proposed that Prasar Bharti and other private channels 
alongwith with agencies like WWF fo r Nature should collaborate and 
increase original Indian content in different languages on our 
television. 
8. No diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes for critical and 
ecologically fragile wildlife habitat shall be allowed. 
103 

RAJYA SABHA [ 15 March, 2002] 
9. Lands falling within 10 kms. of the boundaries of National Parks and 
Sanctuaries should be notified as Eco-fragile zones under section 3(v) of 
the Environment (Protection) Act and Rule 5 Sub-rule 5(viii) & (x) of the 
Environment (Protection) Rules. 
10. Removal of encroachments and illegal activities from within forest lands 
and Protected Areas. 
11. No commercial monoculture to replace natural forests. 
12. The settlement of rights in National Parks and Sanctuaries should not be 
used to exclude or reduce the areas that are crucial and integral part of the 
wildlife habitat. 
13. More than 2000 vacant posts in the frontline staff of Protected Areas shall 
be filled immediately and provided basic infrastructur e for efficient 
discharge of duties. Ban on recruitment of staff against vacant post should 
be lifted on lines with the Police Department. Innovative initiative such as 
redeployment of surplus employees in other departments, hiring local 
people on voluntary or honorarium basis, raising donations from business 
houses and other members of the public in return for a greater role for 
them in implementing programmes need to be explored. 
14. Every protected area should be managed by forest officers trained in 
wildlife management. 
15. Mitigation measures for human-animal conflict and mechanism for crop 
insurance, as also expeditious disbursement of ex-gratia payments should 
be instituted by States. 
16. Forest Commission should be set-up to look into restructuring, reform 
and strengthening the entire forest set up and affiliated institutions in the 
country. 
17. A working group shall be constituted to monitor implementation of 
Wildlife Action-Plan. 
Statement-II 
Salient features of National Wildlife Action Plan 
National Wildlife Action- Plan is a comprehensive document highlighting 
the importance of conservation of natural eco-systems for sustained availability 
of water and meeting the livelihood needs of the people. The Action-Plan gives 
in detail the action required and priority projects that are crucial for effective 
104 

[15 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
conservation of wildlife. The broad parameters covered under the Action-Plan 
are:— 
1. Strengthening and Enhancing the Protected Area Network. 
2. Effective management of Protected Areas. 
3. Conservation of Wild and Endangered Species and their Habitats. 
4. Restoration of degraded habitats outside Protected Areas. 
5. Control of Poaching, Taxidermy and illegal trade in wild animals and 
plant species. 
6. Monitoring and Research. 
7. Human resource development and personnel planning. 
8. Ensuring peoples participation in wildlife conservation. 
9. Conservation awareness and education. 
 
10. Wildlife tourism. 
11. Domestic legislation and international conventions. 
12. Enhancing financial allocation for ensuring sustained fund flow to the 
wildlife sector. 
13. Integration of national Wildlife Action-Plan with other sectoral 
programmes.

Uniform Education 
†l392. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering to abolish the existing dual 
education system and provide uniform education in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government are also considering to provide technical and 
computer science, engineering and medi cal science education to lower class, 
middle class and poor children of rural areas, as being provided to urban children 
and children of rich families; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) and (b). 
The National Policy on Education (NPE), 1986 provides for a National System 
of Education which implies that, up to a given level, all students, irrespective 
of caste, creed, location or sex, have access to education of a comparable quality. 
It includes a common educational structure, a national curriculum framework 
and minimum levels of learning for each stage of education. 
†Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi. 
129 

RAJYA SABHA [ 15 March, 2002] 
(c) and (d) The NPE and its'Programme of Action provide for a definite 
edge for education in rural areas. Pursuant to this, a number of schemes are 
under various stages of implementation, which predominantly address the 
educational needs of rural areas including technical education. 
At the Secondary level, for imparting computer education to students, a 
Scheme viz. Computer Literacy and Studies in Schools is implemented. The 
scheme is proposed to be revamped/r enamed in the X Five Year Plan as 
Information and Computer Technology in  Schools. Other initiatives include 
"Project Vidya" in association with INTEL for training of teachers and 
development of curriculum based software; certificate in computer education 
and X-ray Technicians' course conducted by National Open School etc. In the 
technical education sector, initiatives include strengthening and consolidation 
of infrastructural facilities in engineering and technical education institutions; 
establishment of more engineering and technical education institutions and 
increased intake capacities; establishment of Indian Institute of Information 
Technology (HIT) at Allahabad and Indian Institute of Information Technology 
& Management (IIITM) at Gwalior; increasing output of information technology 
manpower; mobilisation of private initiatives; development of technologies in 
emerging areas and their transfer to  user agencies through technology 
development missions; transfer of techno-economic advances in technical 
education and appropriate technologies to rural people through expansion of 
Community Polytechnics; World Bank assisted Technician Education Project 
and Canada India Institute Industry Linkage Project; constitution of an All 
India Board on Information Technology (IT) Education under All India Council 
for Technical Education etc. Indira Gandhi National Open University is 
providing Internet education through its computer science programmes; 
including an Advanced Diploma in IT, Bachelor in IT etc. through its network 
of regional and study centres spread all over the country. 
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare also follows a Uniform Policy for 
medical science education.

Statement 
Conditions for promotion of Lecturer (Senior Scale) to Lecturer (selection 
Grade/Reader) under Career Advancement Scheme of UGC. 
Lecturer (Selection Grade) 
Lecturers in the Senior Scale who do not have a Ph.D. degree or equivalent 
published work, and who do not meet the scholarship and research standards, 
but fulfil the other criteria given above for the post of Reader, and have a good 
record in teaching and, preferably, have contributed in various ways such as to 
the corporate life of the institution, examination work, or through extension 
activities, will be placed in the Selection Grade, subject to the recommendations 
of the Selection Committee which is the same as for promotion to the post of 
Reader. They will be designated as Lect urers in the Selection Grade. They 
could offer themselves for fresh assessment after obtaining Ph.D. and/or fulfilling 
other requirements for promotion as Reader and, if found suitable, could be 
given the designation of Reader. 
Reader (Promotion) 
A Lecturer in the Senior Scale will be eligible for promotion to the post of 
Reader if she/he has:— 
(i)     Completed 5 years of services in the Senior Scale; 
146 

[15 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii)    Obtained a Ph. D. degree or has equivalent published work; 
(iii) Made some mark in the areas  of scholarship and research as 
evidenced e.g. by self-assessment, reports of referees, quality of 
publications, contribution to educational innovation, design of 
new courses and curricula and extension activities; 
(iv) After placement in the senior Scale participated in two refresher 
courses/summer institutes of approved duration, or engaged in other 
appropriate continuing education programmes of comparable quality 
as may be specified or approved by the University Grants 
Commission; and 
(v)    possesses consistently good performance appraisal reports. 
Promotion to the Post of Reader will be through a process of selection by 
a Selection committee to be set up under the Statutes/Ordinance of the concerned 
University or other similar Committees set up by the appointing authorities. 
If the number of years required in th e feeder cadre are less than those 
stipulated in the UGC's notification thus entailing hardship to those who have 
completed more than the total number of years in their entire service for eligibility 
in the cadre, may be placed in the next  higher grade after adjusting the total 
number of  years.

1414. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of HUMAN

(d) how far this programme has been successful in improving drop-out

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT [DR. (SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The 
National Programme for Nutritional Support to Primary Education commonly 
known as Mid-day Meal Scheme aims to cover all students in classes I—V in 
Government, Govemment-aided and local body schools including schools in 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [ 15 March, 2002] 
backward and tribal areas. At pres ent Gujarat, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and 
Pondicherry are providing cooked meals. 89 tribal blocks of Madhya Pradesh 
and 85 tribal blocks in Chhattisgarh are also providing cooked meals to 
children. In Orissa, cooked meal are being provided in 8 KBK districts and 74 
ITDA blocks of the non-KBK district s. Recently Karnataka has introudced a 
cooked meals in 7 educationally backward  districts of the State. Ready-to-eat 
food is being distributed in Delhi. Th e remaining States/UTs are distributing 
foodgrains (wheat/rice). 
(c) The Government has taken steps to improve the monitoring and 
supervision of the programme at all levels, create a greater awareness regarding 
the programme through involvement of Village Education Committees, 
streamline procedures so as to ensure regular supply of foodgrains and timely 
reimbursement of transportation charge s and payment to Food Corporation 
of India and ensure a more rigorous role for the nodal agency for programme 
implementation at the State level.

programme, Chief Secretaries of States and Administrators of UTs have been 
requested to arrange surprise checks of Primary Schools. Similarly, officers of 
the departments of Elementary Education and Literacy and Secondary & Higher 
Education have also been requested to undertake surprise checks during their 
visits to States/UTs. 
(d) An evaluation has been undertaken in 10 States to asses the efficiency 
and effectiveness of the Programme by  an independent agency, Operations 
Research Group, New Delhi. The study covers Assam, Gujarat, Haryana, Jammu 
& Kashmir, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and 
West Bengal. The report was submitted in September, 1999. The findings of 
the report state that while the programme has given a boost to enrolment in 
Assam, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal; in 6 other States it 
has a positive impact on attendance and retention. 
Besides, a study conducted by NC ERT on State Policies in Incentive 
Schemes in Primary Schools and their Contribution to Girls' participation, 
completed in April 2000, also covers the Mid-day Meal Scheme in Uttar Pradesh 
and Tamil Nadu. The report says that the Noon Meal Scheme of Tamil Nadu 
and supply of foodgrains under MDM in Uttar Pradesh have helped in improve 
the enrolment and retention of girls in schools.

1417. SHRI JIBON ROY: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE

estimated two lakh Nepali girl forced into immoral trafficking in India? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMNT (SHRIMATI SUMITRA MAHAJAN): (a) Yes, Sir.

154 

[15 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
serves as a blueprint for States/UTs for policy and programmatic interventions

1458. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased

ensure availability of FIR forms on running trains to prevent crimes against 
women;

increased during the last few year;

safety of women passengers;

1. Anti-social elements are removed from Railway premises and trains. 
2. Coach Attendants/TTEs keep proper watch on the passengers 
entering/detraining from the coaches. 
3. The coaches are locked during night hours. 
4. FIR forms are made available w ith the Train Guards/Stations

reports immediately.

(b) if so, what are the reasons therefore, when both the countries reportedly 
began research in biotech in agriculture in mid-1980s; 
(c) whether India had genetically modified sixteen agricultural plants, 
but approved for field trials and four for commercialization, whereas the 
comparable figures for China are 141,45 and 31, respectively;  
(d) if so, what are the reasons for so much down trend on biotech research 
in India; and 
(e) what remedial steps are being taken by Government to augment biotech 
in agriculture, on large-scale? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) Yes, Sir. The 
Government is aware of the news item. 
(b) and (c) India entered into biotech research in agriculture in late 80's 
Research was undertaken on the development of several transgenic crops for 
pest resistance, value addition, biotic and abiotic stress resistance in more than 
40 institutions. Under the provisions of Rules, 1989 of Environment 
(Protection)Act, 1986, environmental safety aspects were considered and 
appropriate Biosafety guidelines and institutional mechanisms have been 
established. Indian research efforts have been focused on varieties suitable for 
Indian agro-climatic conditions. China also ventured into this area in mid 80's. 
Their Rules and Guidelines at Nationa l level for conducting research and 
commercialization of transgenic crops  have been formulated recently. A 
number of transgenic crops developed by Indian institutions are at different 
levels of laboratory, green house and field level testing. Crops like Cotton, 
Mustard, Potato, Tomato, Tobacco, Rice Brinjal, Cauliflower and Cabbage are 
at advanced stage of field  trials. No transgenic crop is yet approved for 
commercial release. 
(d) and (e) The agriculture biotechnolo gy research in India is growing 
rapidly at a large number of research institutions being supported by the 
Government. The plant Molecular Biology Programmes has focused on priority 
crops like Cotton, Mustard, Wheat and Rice and other legumes. A national 
Centre for Plant Genome Research is focusing on sequencing the genome of

Chickpea. A National Research Centre on Plant Biotechnology at Indian 
Agricultural Research Institute (IAR1), New Delhi, has been conducting plant 
biotechnology research. India is also partner in the International Rice Genome 
Sequencing Project. Towards the use of  transgenics, a National Transgenic 
Containment and Quarantine Facility at National Bureau of Plant Genetic 
Resources (NBPGR), New Delhi has been setup to facilitate research taking 
care of all biosafety aspects. Government is also supporting M.Sc. course in 
Agricultural Biotechnology in 7 Agricultural Universitie s to generate skilled 
human resource. The biosafety procedures have been further streamlined with 
185 Institutional Biosafety Committees. (IBSCs) already established in various 
research institutions and Industrial Research & Development units. With the 
accelerated pace of research in transgenics, field trials of Mustard, Potato, Brinjal 
and Tomato are very promising.

1469. SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of 
YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose a long term plan for sponsorship of specific

sports to the Private sector;

country, so far? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF YOUTH AFFAIRS 
AND SPORTS (SHRI P. RADHAKIRISHNAN): (a) to (e) With the idea of inviting support 
and cooperation of the Corporate sector in promoting excellence in sports in active 
partnership with Government and National Sports Federations (NSFs) and to initiate a 
fruitful dialogue between the Government and the Industry in the interest of sports 
promotion, a meeting was held on 7th December, 2001 under the Chairmanship of 
Hon'ble Finance Minister with the representatives of the Chambers of Commerce and 
Industry. Though the private sector is making a useful contribution in promotion of 
sports, the meeting was 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [15 March, 2002] 
held to obtain support of the industry in a planned manner. It was decided to 
adopt the following course of action:

the Government and Industry in the interest of promotion of sports. 
(ii) Scouting talent is of crucial importance for grooming sportspersons 
who can excel at the international level. Therefore, both the 
Government and the Industry must exchange notes regarding talent 
scouting and take follow up action to nurture such talent. 
(iii) An action plan should be prepared in respect of the possible area of 
cooperation between he Government and the Industry. 
(iv) Representatives of Industry Associations and Government should 
periodically review the progress made in promoting sports with the 
active participation of the Industry associations.

The Plight of Fishermen in Tamil Nadu on the Coast of Bay of 
Bengal 
SHRI P.N. SIVA (Tamil Nadu): Sir, the fishermen living on the 
cost of Bay of Bengal, in Nagapattinam, Pudukottai and Ramnad 
Districts of Tamil Nadu, being treated brutally and inhumanly by the Sri 
Lankan Navy personnel, when they are out for fishing, has become a 
day-to-day occurrence. Two me chanised boats, TJC 947MB and 
QDMS1314MS, which left the Nagapattinam Jetty on 15.2.02 at about 
22.30 hrs., and which should have returned by the 17 th February 
morning, have not returned at all. It is learnt from other fishermen that 
these boats were taken away by the Sri Lankan Navy, along with 
twelve fishermen on board. The condition of these fishermen is not 
known. The suffering of these fi shermen at the hands of the Sri 
Lankan Navy, while in their custody, is so horrible to believe. The 
fishermen who are caught are made to swim along with the speeding 
boat, tied to a rope. Those who are not able to swim at this speed are 
taken into the boat and beaten severely with the butts of guns and are 
forced to hold the hot silencer of the boat. A series of such incidents 
has scared the fishermen to such an extent that they refrain from going 
out for fishing, resulting in the starvation of their families and a heavy 
revenue loss for the Government. The Union Government's 
intervention is an urgent need of the hour for finding a permanent 
solution to prevent a recurrence  of these dreadful events and to 
release the twelve fishermen from the custody of the Sri Lankan Navy. 
The Government has to save their lives. 
Sir, I do not know about the developments which might have 
taken place after I gave my notice. Since the hon. External Affairs 
Minister is here, I would like to know from him what steps the 
Government is taking for finding a permanent solution to this problem.

Sethu Samudram Scheme 
SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU (Pondicherry): The Sethu 
Samudram Canal Project was conc eived more than 140 years ago. 
This project was conceived even prior to the scheme of Suez Canal. 
Sir, 3,555 miles of Indian coast runs from the East to the West to 
enable the Indian ships to navigate within the Indian territorial waters.   
Prior to Independence, 
219 

RAJYA SABHA [15 MARCH, 2002]  
several Committees were appointed to ascertain the feasibility of the 
Sethu Samudram Scheme. In 1955, the Ramasamy Mudaliyar 
Committee estimated its cost at Rs. 9.98 crores. Subsequently, the 
Nagendra Singh Committee, the Venkateswaran Committee, the 
Technical Committee of the Government of India and several other 
Committee were appointed. A feasibilit y report was al so prepared. It 
was also included in the Ninth Five Year Plan. On 2.2.2001, the hon. 
Prime Minister assured that the promise made by the NDA 
Government for early completion of the project would be fulfilled. We 
were shocked to know that India and Sri Lanka have decided to 
construct a Hanuman Bridge across the Palk Straits-Sethu 
Samudram. If this bridge is constructed, it would prove to be a Berlin 
Wall and stall the Sethu Samudram Project. My apprehension is that 
the declaration made by the Indian Pr ime Minister and the Sri Lankan 
Prime Minister would give a decent burial to the Sethu Samudram 
Scheme. If a bridge is constructed, it would not be possible to use the 
canal for navigation purpose. On the other hand, if the canal is built 
near the Adams Bridge linking the Palk Straits with Gulf of Mannar, 
we can have an international seaway . Sentimentally, we can call it a 
Hanuman Sethu Samudram Canal. Therefore, I request the 
Government not to construct a bridge on the canal. Thank you.

Visakhapatnam Steel Plant in my hom e State, Andhra Pradesh, is the 
only shore-based integrated steel plant, away from MOKAMA apart

has the advantage of easier import of raw materials and export of 
finished products. This plant provides employment opportunities in my 
home State and it also plays a key role  in its economy. However, this 
plant is sick because of the slowdow n in the steel sector and due to

transportation costs, it will take time for its completion. A revival 
package for this plant is overdue; the same is getting delayed for one 
reason or the other. The Government has already gone ahead with a 
revival package for SAIL, but the Vizag Steel Plant is being 
discriminated against, in the matter of revival. Now, the Government is

Utilisation of amount realised through Disinvestment 
SHRI LAJPAT RAI (Punjab): Si r, since 1991, the Government 
of India has been disinvesting in various public sector undertakings. 
The amount realised from disinvestment is not shown in budgetary 
revenue and, as such, it is not expected to be accounted for in 
budgetary receipts. An amount of Rs. 18,638 crores has been 
received till 2000, and much more than that, during 2000-2001 and 
2001-2002, by way of disinvestment in PSUs. The amount to be 
received or collected by way of di sinvestment cannot be calculated in 
advance, as the process is contro lled by various extraneous factors 
and, as such, utilisation cannot be pre-planned. Moreover, the 
expenditure on social welfare activities has to be met separately, even 
if the disinvestment process is not ther e or it fails to meet the required 
amount. As the Members of this august House know fully well, per 
capita debt in our country is growing day by day and there is no 
concrete and clear-cut policy or plan to check this ever-increasing, 
unhealthy, economic trend. It is a known fact that these PSUs had 
been set up by taking huge amounts on loan, which could not be paid 
back till today. It is, t herefore, strongly propos ed that the amount 
realised by way of disinvestment should be kept in reserve and it 
should be used only for paying back the huge debts that have piled up 
over the years, of course, after meeting the direct charge on VRS, etc. 
Trafficking in Children 
PROF. (SHRIMATI) BHARATI RAY (West Bengal): Sir, I bring 
to the notice of this august House a growing ulcer in our body-politic. 
Its name is human trafficking. Ne xt to arms and drugs, women 
trafficking is the largest form of transnational organised crime; and 
these three are connected financially and organisationally. I want to 
specially mention about trafficking in children. We talk of children's 
rights, human rights and women's em powerment, but these are mere 
words when thousands of girl children are used in the most odious of 
all trades, flesh trade. It is the most extreme form of violation of 
human rights and objectification of women. Most victims come from 
socially and economically backward classes arid are sold and resold, 
yielding multiple profits. Indi a signed the SAARC Convention Against 
Trafficking in Children, but nothing is being done to implement it. 
Commercial sexual exploitation is increasing; sex tourism is 
fashionable; existing laws are tota lly inadequate; victims are hardly 
rehabilitated; traffickers and procurers are rarely apprehended. No 
manual exists on trafficking;   no   details   about   how   diseases   like   
AIDS   spread   through

SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA (TAMIL NADU): Sir, there have been 
widespread reports about the proposed amendments to the legal 
frameworks of the country, which have regulated industrial relations 
since Independence. These amendments have been opposed by the 
trade unions across the country as well as by various political parties.

Industrial Disputes Act is to enhance  the limit of workers from. 100 to 
1000 so that these establishm ents can go in for closure and 
retrenchment of the workers, without seeking Government's 
permission. The second thing is to make the framework more flexible 
by which the labour can be engaged on flexible terms and can be 
easily terminated. The objective seems to be to encourage private 
sector investment in labour-intensive and export-oriented industries, by 
making it easier for prospective employers to hire and fire. In that 
case, there is no scope for labour being treated with dignity and they 
will be at the mercy of the employer s, which will be a se rious threat to 
the labour sector and the human res ource available in our country. It 
will lead to further unemployment, as there is already abundant labour 
in the market;.it will also give rise to  serious social In security, which is 
to be addressed with immediate effect. I, therefore, urge upon the 
Government to take note of this serious concern raised by the trade 
unions and labour organisations and to give a second thought to the 
proposed amendments.

Salt Satyagraha in Orissa - Appeal for Centres Intervention 
DR. M.N. DAS (Orissa): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, an age-old 
occupation of the coastal population of Orissa had been preparing salt 
from seawater and its export outside. But with the British occupation in 
1803, the East India Company denied  that economic privilege to 
people and carried on salt manufacture and trade by its agents. It was 
not for nothing that when Mahatma Gandhi launched the Salt 
Satyagraha in 1930, Orissa played the most prominent role in breaking 
the salt law of the British. Today thousands of families who earn their 
livelihood from manufacture of common salt are threatened with 
regulation that only iodised-salt should be consumed by the people. It 
is like a bolt from the blue. Nobody would deny medicinal value of 
iodised-salt. But the companies pu rchase common salt from the poor 
producers at one rupee per kg. But after this salt is iodised; its price 
becomes seven rupee per kg. Can the poor afford such an exorbitant 
price charged by profit-making enterprises? People have been 
threatening to launch a second salt Satyagraha to defy the order. It 
has been said that wrong information is being circulated regarding the 
bad effect of common salt vis-a-vis the good effect of iodised-salt. Nine 
organisations have already started a movement against the sale of 
iodised-salt. At a place named Humma eleven thousand tonnes of 
common salt is being wasted because of this ban imposed by the 
Government. The salt manufacturers are starving. Unrest coupled with 
law and order problem may soon take shape. I appeal to the Union 
Government for immediate intervention to solve the crisis. The interests 
of poor salt manufacturers need protection while iodising the common 
salt at a minimum cost. The common people must not suffer for the 
profit-making of private companies.

Suicide by Farmers in the Country 
DR. Y. RADHAKRISHNA MURTY (ANDHRA PRADESH): Sir, 
my Special Mention is relating to the pathetic stories of suicides 
committed by farmers in the country .  These stories are pouring in 
everyday. 
Peasants cultivating paddy in  Punjab, cotton in Andhra 
Pradesh and Karnataka, groundnut in Andhra Pradesh are becoming 
desperate to the extent of ending  their own lives, as they are 
increasingly falling into a debt trap. 
There is a lack of proper extension services, scarce public 
credit, higher interest rates by t he private money lenders, unchecked 
supply of spurious seeds and pesticides, non-availability of 
remunerative prices, untimely intervention by the FCI, CCI, OILFED, 
etc. The cumulative effect of a ll these avoidable factors lead to the 
miserable condition of small peas ants and thereby pushing them to 
take the extreme step of ending their own lives. 
Sir, the districts of Warangal , Anantapur and Karimnagar of 
Andhra Pradesh are the worst hit. Sir, Anantapur district alone 
recorded fifteen such deaths - and more since I gave notice for this 
Special Mention - in the first six weeks of the current year. Reports 
from Karimnagar district reveal two such cases during the last two or 
three days. I have enclosed a report on this. 
The Human Rights Council, Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, 
has sought the intervention of the National Human Rights Commission 
to institute an inquiry; and awar d compensation to the families of 
victims. The Secretary, in his Me morandum, said that during the last 
three years, in twenty districts of  Andhra Pradesh, 638. farmers ended 
their lives, due to crop failure and due to other resultant losses. 
The Council further said that out of 490 suicides reported in 
the country during 2001-2002, 385 were from Andhra Pradesh. 
The plight of kisan in various parts of the country, particularly 
those growing commercial crops, is pitiable. 
The crisis in agriculture has to be attended to on an 
emergency basis. 
A high-level expert Committee should be appointed to have an 
in-depth study on this problem and payment of ex-gratia to the kin of 
the

Request to extend guarantee to bonds raised by 
State Government of Andhra Pradesh 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, my 
Special Mention pertains to a request to extend guarantee to the 
bonds being raised by the Government of Andhra Pradesh. 
Andhra Pradesh has 48 per cent share in the total seafood 
exports worth Rs.6,400 crores from t he country. In spite of this, since 
1997, the plight of the seafood exporters of A.P. has become 
miserable. Their problems were discussed at several fora but in vain. 
After persistent requests and demands from the Government of 
Andhra Pradesh, and seafood exporter s, the Ministry of Commerce 
and Industry has appointed the IIM, Kolkata, to find out a solution for 
this problem. The IIM recommended the creation of a Reconstruction 
Fund through raising bonds and levying a 2 per cent cess on future 
exports to repay the bonds. As this recommendation affects the 
interests of new promoters of  aqua culture, MPEDA and the 
Commerce Ministry have slightly modified this recommendation to 
assist the new industries, up to a maximum of Rs. 1.5 crores. As per 
this recommendation, the Governm ent of Andhra Pradesh decided to 
raise bonds worth Rs. 700 crores from the market to create a 
Reconstruction Fund, to bail out seafood exporters of Andhra Pradesh. 
I request the Government of India to accede to the request of the 
Government of Andhra Pradesh whic h -is not asking the Centre to 
shell out any money, but only request ing to extend guarantee to the 
bonds raised by

SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, I rise to speak on the Motion of Thanks on the 
President's Address delivered to both the Houses of Parliament on 
25th February, 2002. At the outset, I appeal to all the people, 
especially, the VHP and other organisations, to abide by the Supreme 
Court judgement as far as Ayodhya is concerned. Sir, we, in the TDP, 
have always felt that the issue, which has been taunting this nation, is 
of no relevance today. We cannot expect to rewrite the 500-year old 
history now. Let us use all our energies to fight the economic 
deprivation that the country is facing and make the country 
economically stronger. Really, the President of India - and the Finance 
Minister, in his Budget has given a very rosy picture. My speech will 
be based mainly on the extracts fr om various documents that have 
been supplied by the Government - th e Economic Survey of India, the 
Mid-term Appraisal, the CAG Report; nothing more than that. I am not 
giving my own opinion. I have drawn conclusions based on those 
extracts and the information furnished in these documents. 
Sir, the economy has been passing through the worst crisis 
since the post independence era. We had set some targets in the 
Ninth Plan, which we could not ac hieve. Various, reasons have been 
given. But let us go into the facts. We have failed to achieve the 
targets that have been stipulated for every sector — agriculture, 
industry, infrastructure, foreign trade and so on. As against the target 
of 6.5 per cent growth rate fixed in the Ninth Plan, it is now evident that 
if we are able to can achieve more than 5.2 per cent, it is going to be a 
very big achievement. Sir, a 0.1 per cent rise in the growth rate makes 
a hell of a difference in the economy. The Economic Survey has done 
a commendable job by presenting the figures pertaining to growth 
rates. The Survey, in para 1108 conf irms, "As a result, the combined 
fiscal deficit of the States and the Central Government together, 
accounting for more than 10 per cent of the GDP, has pushed up the 
debt servicing and, in the process, inhibited the ability of the 
Government to undertake necessary expenditure for investment in the 
provision of public services, which,  in turn, becomes responsible for 
the slow down of the private sector ". The observation made by Shri 
Montek Singh Ahluwalia, in his report, is, "There is a strong 
complementality between   public   investment   and   private   
investment,   which   will   have

SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU) (Rajasthan): Mr. 
Vice-Chairman, Sir, I thank you for giving me this opportunity. Sir, 
while I share the sentiments of the House in thanking the hon. 
President for the Address given to the Parliament, I stand to oppose 
the same and would like to point out certain inadequacies and certain 
very important issues that should have been covered in this policy 
statement of the Government of India. 
Sir, on the 8 th of March every year, we celebrate the 
International Women's Day with great speeches and promises for 
upliftment of women, and while 2002 has been declared as the 
Women's Empowerment Year, I am pained and sad to note that there 
is absolutely no reference whatsoever in the President's Address on 
issues which effect status of women. While the women share a 
substantial burden in the rural ar eas and economy, their issues have 
been totally ignored. 
The Constitutional Amendment Bill providing for reservation of 
seats for women in the State Legisl atures and Parliament has been 
pending for far too long. I can see no reason why a consensus cannot 
be arrived at. A number of parties including Congress Party have 
promised support to pass this B ill, yet the Government has shown a 
total lack of interest. We would be failing in our duty to the people of 
India if this Bill is not passed in the current Session of Parliament. 
The hon. President of India, in his address to the nation on the 
eve of the Republic Day this year has expressed serious concern over 
atrocities against the female child and women. He stressed that a 
female child is not even safe in the womb of the mother. I suggest that 
strict provisions be made for prevention of female foeticide. 
I am happy that a Bill has been introduced in the Parliament 
for prevention of domestic violence against women. This Bill should be 
passed immediately. Strict provisions must be included for its effective 
implementation. 
The Supreme Court had observed about three years back that 
firm steps be taken for prevention of sexual abuse of women at place 
places of work and had given an elaborate scheme in that regard. I am 
surprised that the Government has not yet brought forth a legislation 
to prevent harassment and sexual abuse of women at places of work.

controlled environment for sexual related cases should be formalised

poverty that still remains in different parts of the country manifested in 
sale of women and children. While a separate Ministry of Poverty 
Alleviation has been set up by the Go vernment of India, it still has to 
implement the various schemes.

practicing their own faith. In this co nnection, I would like to know from

We have seen in the recent past the role of the police in the 
communal riots in Gujarat. The minority community is very 
inadequately represented in the police and paramilitary forces, which 
adds a sense of insecurity in t he minds of the minorities in the

So, I strongly urge upon the Government to recruit minorities 
into the forces on the basis of proportional representation or on some 
other similar formula, to give them  confidence in the Government and 
a sense of active participation. 
If I recall correctly, the Rapid Action Force was constituted with 
the specific objective of handling communal riots. It was decided that 
33 per cent of the force would cons ist of members from the minority 
communities. But I regret to say that even here, the rule has not been 
adhered to. 
In the President's Address, the Government has mentioned 
about the anti-terrorism legislation called POTO. Our past experience 
with such draconian laws has been very bitter. When the Chief Minister 
of Gujarat makes statements that  the POTO would be applied for in 
the case of particular heinous incident and not in the case of other 
similar heinous incidents which occurred subsequently, raises serious 
doubts in the minds of the people about the bonafides of the 
Government. As mentioned earlier, the minorities are already 
subjected to harassment and are being needlessly and cruelly targeted 
by the security agencies. I urge upon the Union Government to keep 
that in mind before going ahead with this Bill as this will be a major 
cause of concern for a large number of people.

SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA (Karnataka): Sir, while 
addressing the Joint Session, the hon. President has laid stress on the 
terrorist activities, the terrorist attack on Indian Parliament and cross-
border terrorism. He has also highlighted how the development of the 
country has slowed down. The major share of our economy has been 
diverted to maintain the border security and vigilance, and to contain 
the terrorist activities. He has also mentioned the steps taken by the 
Government in this regard. 
Another point he has highlighted is the way Pakistan's 
nefarious designs and its abetment of terrorist activities has been 
exposed. 
The next point highlighted by him is the maintenance of 
communal harmony. He has mention ed the various issues that have 
arisen out of the Ayodhya dispute, what its effects will be on the 
common people if th,e dispute remains unsolved for long, what the 
objectives and achievements of the Government are, and what type of 
development is necessary for upli ftment of the poor and the needy 
people. 
So far as the terrorist activities and attacks are concerned, the 
Government has taken correct steps in  that direction, to curtail the 
activities of the terrorists and to ex pose, in the international fora, the 
involvement of Pakistan in the attack on Indian Parliament. So far as 
communal harmony is concerned, it is  my feeling, and it is also the 
feeling of the country, that the 
266 

[15 MARCH, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
Government is not acting properly or  is not taking steps, in the right 
direction, to maintain communal harmony.   I do condemn the heinous        
act at Godhra.   At the same time, I strongly condemn the aftermath of 
the Godhra  killings also. It was the duty of the Government to have 
anticipated the backlash from the Godhra incident. Whatever has 
happened in Gujarat, the  prestige of the whole country in the eyes of 
the world has come down. 
So far as the other aspects are concerned, the President has 
completely left them out. For example, he has not mentioned about 
the economic development, the condition of the people and the 
problems of unemployment and corruption. He has emphasised only 
two or three points. Development has been given a go-by. 
As stated earlier, he has highli ghted only two issues. All the 
other issues have been neglected. Now, I want to make a point 
regarding the agriculturists. Agriculturists who constitute 68 per cent 
of the population, are giving a lot of employment to the majority of our 
population, but due to a fall in the prices of their products, they are not 
able to get even the cost of producti on, and they are forced to commit 
suicide. For the past two or three years, the farmers all over the 
country are committing suicide, but this Government has not come to 
their rescue. It has not come out with specific programmes and 
policies to save the farmers. 
The next point I am going to highlight is the unemployment 
problem. The rural unemployment is becoming acute day by day. The 
farmers are not getting employment. There are no better employment 
opportunities for them. There are no new sources of income for them. 
It is the policy of the Government to disinvest the public sector 
undertakings and to close down the industries. But they have not 
created any new avenues of employment. 
Under these circumstances, wh ere are the youths of this 
country being taken by the Government? Youths have no future in this 
country. They cannot get employ ment and, therefore, they cannot 
prosper. 
The Family Planning Programme was started 30 years back, 
but still there is a continuous growth of population. This is a very 
important aspect which is hampering  the development of our country. 
The programmes which have been started are not sufficient to contain 
the population growth. The President has not touched on this issue in 
his Address. The Government should have given thrust to it. 
267 

RAJYA SABHA           [15 MARCH, 2002]  
So far as electricity is concer ned, the country, as a whole, is 
facing a severe power problem, particularly in the rural areas. Even if 
power is there, the voltage is very  low. The farmers are suffering. 
Sometimes, they remain without power for days together. Therefore, 
they are not able to cultivate their land. This issue has also not found 
a.place in the President's Address. 
In the age of globalisation, t he small-scale industries have 
been closed down and production has stopped in village and small-
scale industries. The Government should have taken some steps to 
revive the village and small-scale industries. The banks have started 
giving financial assistance to the small-scale industries. But this 
measure is not sufficient to revive the small-scale industries. 
Sir, even after 55 years of Independence, villagers are not 
getting potable water. After the in troduction of the Panchayati Raj 
System we could see some bore we lls in villages. But due to lack of 
fluoride content, a majority of the villages are not getting potable 
drinking water. That is also one of the problems. The Government 
should have taken care of it and prepared a special plan in this regard. 
My next point relates to health. Private hospitals are coming 
up only in cities. In villages and Talukas, people are not able to get 
proper treatment. People are dying. No medicines are available in the 
village hospitals. There are no doctors. The President has not made 
any reference to this problem in his Address. The Government should 
have taken specific care in this regard. Merely opening some hospitals 
is not sufficient. These hospitals should have all the facilities and 
medicines should also be available in  these hospitals. Sir, today, you 
go to any hospital in any State, y ou go to any Primary Health Centre, 
you will see that no medicine is available there.  The people are 
suffering. 
The Ninety-Third Amendment gives the right to education to 
children in the age group of 6-14 years. The quality of teachers in 
villages is a matter of serious* concern. If one goes to the UPSC or to 
the State Public Service Commission, they look at the Marksheet first. 
But, the standard of education is different in villages and cities. In 
cities, high-tech education is being imparted; whereas, in villages, 
children are not getting the same type of education. That is why they 
are not selected for such jobs. 
 268 

[15 MARCH, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
Earlier, some States were giving rural weightage in the matter 
of selection; but this has been stru ck down by the Court. It is a great 
injustice caused to the rural youth, who come from a poor 
background, whose parents are illiterate. Under these circumstances, 
it is essential that weightage is given in the matter of employment 
opportunities to these rural folks; we can also have a quota fixed for 
them. 
Then, as regards fast track courts, the Government did take 
sufficient steps to establish fast track courts. But the courts are not 
able to dispose of the cases at the speed with which the cases should 
have been disposed of. In this context, I draw the attention of the hon. 
Law Minister to the fact that there are several cases, right from 
matrimonial and maintenance cases, which are pending before the 
various courts, and the disposal of these cases take six-seven years' 
time. Under these circumstances, the number of fast strack courts has to 
be increased and the Government must see to it that the cases are 
disposed of as early as possible. 
Sir, in the President's Address, there should have also been a 
mention about the establishment of a Bench of the Supreme Court in 
the Southern part of the country. It is very important that a Supreme 
Court Bench is set up there, as the Southern region of our country is 
coming up in a big way. In this connection, I suggest that Karnataka 
would be the most suitable place for this, as it is accessible to all other 
places of the South, namely, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala; it 
is also accessible to Goa. Moreover, in the matter of infrastructure, we 
have a first-class court building. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI T. N. CHATURVEDI) : Your time 
is over. You have to wind up now. 
SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA : I am concluding, Sir. I urge upon 
the Government to think over this matter. I am not saying this just for 
the sake of it. But it is very im portant that a Benc h of the Supreme 
Court is to be set up in this part of the country. This would not only 
save a lot of precious time and money of the common people, but it 
would also help them in getting justice at their doorstep. So, this 
should be looked into very, seriously and the Government s hould 
consider setting up of a Bench at Bangalore. 
Finally, I would like to say that  the President's Address has 
not touched upon another important pr oblem that is having its impact 
on every aspect of our economy, and t hai is, corruption. Corruption is 
spreading like AIDS. Nobody is ready to deal with it.. It is swallowing the 
entire developmental money which is earmarked in the Plan and Non-
Plan outlays.     Hence the 
269 

RAJYA SABHA [15 MARCH, 2002]  
Government should take strict steps to see to it that corruption is 
eradicated from our society. Otherwise, whatever we propose in the 
outlay would not be available for productive purposes and the money 
would just be drained away. With these words, I conclude.

SHRI SHANKAR ROY CHOWDHURY  (West Bengal): Sir, I 
would like to emphasize just on one issue, that is, regarding the 
governance of the country, which has not been covered in the 
President's Address. 
Eighty per cent or ninety per cent of the task of governance of 
the country, it appears, is in the hands of States and not more than ten 
to fifteen per cent in the hands of the Centre. The Centre lays down 
the policy, and it is for the States to implement it. I think, at the root of 
all our problems -- whether it is security, whether it is economics, 
whether it is our social structure or any other issue that affects the 
nation, as a whole, ultimately devolves upon the management of 
national governance. But what we are seeing, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, 
is this. I have been going through the President's Addresses since 
1999 and I find that Centre-State relations have been mentioned only 
once.    What we are seeing day by day, in a

pluralistic, multi-cultural, multi-polit ical environment in this country, is 
that the relations between the Cent re and the States have become so

or on social grounds or on socio-economic grounds. What is the 
answer to all our problems? The President's Address has indicated 
what the Central Government has been doing to see to it that in its 
own way, from its own point of view , in its own perception, what the

implemented at the level where it t ouches the life of the people. So, I

Government as well as the State Government - the Governments at

Central Government, not withstanding political differences, economic 
differences and increasingly personal differences - should devise 
some method of pulling together for the benefit of citizens of this 
country.

methpd is somehow rationalised, the be st plans, call them Five Year 
Plans, the best policies will be uni mplementable at the grass root 
levels, where it affects the lives of the people throughout the length 
and breadth of the country. The next is sue I wish to speak on is the
